title: Programmable, durable plant immunity against diverse pathogens

concept.text: The innovation would be a reliable way to design disease resistance for different crops: choose pathogen features that plants should recognize, install or adapt receptors that detect those features, and connect detection to effective defenses. The intended capability extends beyond producing an individual resistant variety. It would make resistance to diverse pathogens a systematically designable trait while preserving productive growth and maintaining protection as pathogen populations evolve.

One technical foundation is the plant pattern-recognition receptor, which detects molecular features shared by microbes. Features important to microbial physiology may be harder for pathogens to change without a cost, although they are not evolution-proof. Recognition alone is insufficient: a transferred receptor must also cooperate with the recipient plant’s signaling machinery. The supplied study describes engineering the receptor’s C-terminal region to strengthen its interaction with the signaling partner SOBIR1 while retaining recognition by its external domain. This illustrates how recognition and signaling compatibility can be adjusted separately, without establishing that every receptor can be made functional in every crop.

significance.text: If this capability became broadly transferable and durable, crop disease resistance could be developed through a repeatable engineering process: identify useful recognition targets, adapt receptors to the crop, and verify effective protection. The revolutionary step would be reliable control over that process across crop families and pathogen groups. Receptor transfer and domain engineering provide an experimental foundation for this possibility, but the demonstrated examples do not yet establish that level of generality.

Conditional downstream possibilities include more dependable harvests, reduced disease losses and less reliance on some chemical disease-control treatments. These are prospective consequences, not outcomes established by the supplied experiments. Their scale would depend on which diseases are controlled, how resistance performs under farm conditions, how quickly pathogens adapt, and whether protection carries yield or ecological costs. Neither a single resistance gene nor resistance to several experimental challenges implies elimination of pesticide use.

The analogy to programming has limits. A receptor is a biological component operating within a species-specific network, and its behavior depends on compatible partners, expression and downstream defense responses. The study’s unsuccessful transfers and species-specific effects show why a useful receptor cannot simply be assumed to work wherever it is introduced. Durable immunity would also have to remain effective against changing pathogen populations, extending the challenge beyond initial receptor design.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability is a general design process that combines difficult-to-evade recognition, effective signaling in different crops, acceptable growth costs and sustained protection. The supplied study addresses parts of this problem, but does not demonstrate the complete capability. Its evidence also cannot determine whether subsequent work has resolved particular barriers.

Recognition must target pathogen features whose conservation makes escape difficult, while remaining useful against the pathogens that actually threaten the crop. Conserved microbial patterns offer a rationale for broader recognition, but conservation does not guarantee that a pathogen cannot evade detection or otherwise overcome defense. Resistance to a tested set of organisms therefore needs to be distinguished from resistance across unrelated pathogen classes and from evolutionary durability.

A second barrier is compatibility between the introduced receptor and the recipient plant’s signaling machinery. Strengthening the RLP–SOBIR1 interaction supplies one engineering approach, but species-specific failures indicate that additional factors matter. Successful signaling in isolated cells is only an intermediate result: it must translate into protection in intact plants, relevant tissues and disease conditions.

Defense must also be activated without unacceptable costs to development or productivity. The study describes dwarfism associated with adaptor coexpression, illustrating that increasing immune activity can create growth penalties. Its reported absence of a detected tomato fruit-yield penalty in one experiment is encouraging, but does not establish acceptable costs across varieties, environments or seasons. Long-term stability and field performance remain explicit future directions in the paper.

current_state.text: Yang, Steidele, Huang and colleagues’ “Engineered pattern recognition receptors enhance broad-spectrum plant resistance” was published online on 13 October 2025, according to the publication history identified in the supplied review. The document also carries October 2026 issue pagination; the online publication date is the appropriate date for describing when this result was reported. The supplied freshness record is empty, so this study cannot establish the field’s overall status as of 1 November 2026 or exclude later advances.

The reviewed text reports that stable expression of RLP23 in tomato increased resistance to tested bacterial, fungal and oomycete pathogens: Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000, Botrytis cinerea and Phytophthora infestans. C-terminal receptor engineering further improved resistance in the reported experiments. These were controlled growth and infection studies. Breadth here means protection against the tested organisms from three microbial groups within this experimental system, not established protection against all members of those groups.

The study also reports no detected fruit-yield penalty in the reported tomato experiment, enhanced immune signaling in rice protoplasts, and enhanced fungal resistance in transiently expressing poplar leaves. These findings have different scopes. Rice protoplast signaling does not establish disease resistance in an intact rice plant, and transient expression in poplar leaves does not establish stable, inherited resistance in whole trees. The tomato yield result likewise does not demonstrate that defense costs will remain negligible under other conditions.

Long-term field durability was not demonstrated in this study; the authors identify long-term stability and field performance as future work. That conclusion concerns the supplied study, rather than proving that no field-durability result exists elsewhere. The evidence supports a technical foundation for programmable immunity while leaving the larger proposed capability unestablished.

The supplied review relied on a partially extracted PDF: substantial results and methods were readable, but pages 10–12 had no extracted text, and original figures and supplementary material were not inspected. Some infection timings in figure captions and Methods differ, so precise assay timing cannot be confidently reconstructed from this review. These limitations constrain verification of the underlying data without negating the readable qualitative findings. The supplied material also does not verify the earlier account of an HTML sign-in redirect or the historical PDF-access sequence.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independent groups should use a documented design process to produce resistance to unrelated pathogen classes in several crop families. The central test would be whether the process transfers predictably, with receptor choice, compatibility engineering and expected protection specified before the final disease challenges. Whole-plant disease outcomes would be required; isolated-cell signaling and transient leaf assays would provide supporting evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Predictable whole-plant resistance across unrelated pathogen classes and crop families

completion_criteria.text: Proposed durability evaluation: test engineered crops across multiple seasons and locations, with appropriate susceptible and existing-resistance comparators. Monitor pathogen populations and changes in resistance performance, and investigate any apparent escape. This proposal extends the paper’s stated need for long-term stability and field evaluation, but its particular replication requirements are not an established standard endorsed by the source.
completion_criteria.label: Resistance durability tested across multiple seasons and locations

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical evaluation: measure disease severity, pathogen burden, harvestable yield, developmental effects and defense-related costs under both disease pressure and low-disease conditions. Include monitoring of beneficial organisms as an ecological safeguard. Predefine success thresholds, observation periods and acceptable tradeoffs for each crop and disease context, and make methods and results sufficiently available for independent reproduction. No particular numerical threshold or duration is established by the supplied material.
completion_criteria.label: Reproducible practical evaluations measure crop outcomes against predefined success thresholds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reporting boundary: a successful demonstration should state the crop families, varieties, pathogens, environments and duration actually tested, together with failures and conditions requiring further adaptation. Finite experiments can establish demonstrated breadth and durability over an observed interval; they cannot establish literal universality or permanent immunity against future pathogen evolution.
completion_criteria.label: Demonstrated resistance breadth and durability reported with experimental limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: BOT-04, “An inexpensive, broadly transferable method to edit and regenerate plants,” could provide a route for installing engineered immune components across crops. BOT-03, “Whole-plant synthetic genome construction and rewriting,” could permit more extensive redesign of immune networks. Both concern enabling construction capabilities; BOT-08 concerns whether the resulting plants recognize pathogens, resist disease and retain productive growth over time.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-05, “Predictive plant biology from genome to whole-organism performance,” overlaps with predicting receptor compatibility and defense–growth tradeoffs. BOT-12, “A causal map of plant-wide communication and plasmodesmatal control,” overlaps with understanding how defense responses are coordinated across tissues. These concepts could inform immunity design, but their goals extend beyond pathogen resistance, and BOT-08 requires disease and durability demonstrations of its own.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-01, “Nitrogen-fixing partnerships for major cereal crops,” and BOT-16, “Predictable control of plant–mycorrhizal nutrient exchange,” concern beneficial microbial relationships. Their relevant connection is the need to understand whether engineered pathogen recognition affects useful plant–microbe interactions. They remain distinct goals: controlling nutrient partnerships does not establish disease resistance, and disease resistance does not establish successful symbiosis.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-14, “Programmable, multigenerational epigenetic inheritance of adaptive plant traits,” overlaps with persistence of useful traits across generations. Its central challenge is control of inherited epigenetic states. BOT-08’s durability additionally concerns continued protection as pathogens evolve; stable inheritance of an immune trait alone would not establish that protection.

Roster-based synthesis: BOT-09, “Affordable preservation and recovery of exceptional plant diversity,” could preserve biological diversity relevant to discovering or breeding disease resistance. Preserving that diversity and engineering a repeatable immune-design process are separate achievements. BOT-07, “Transferable resurrection-like desiccation tolerance in productive crops,” shares the challenge of transferring a protective capability while retaining productivity, but addresses water-loss stress rather than pathogen recognition.

brief.title: Lasting crop protection designed to resist many diseases
possible: Farmers could grow crops with disease protection tailored to their needs that lasts as disease-causing microbes evolve. Researchers could choose microbial warning signs and equip crops with matching receptors, proteins that detect those signs and trigger defenses.
why: A repeatable way to design resistance could give farmers more dependable harvests, reduce disease losses and lessen reliance on some chemical disease treatments. Crop breeders could adapt the same design process to different crops and diseases.

sources.who: Yuankun Yang, Christina E. Steidele, Xianlong Huang and colleagues
sources.showed: Moving a receptor into tomatoes increased resistance to tested bacteria, fungi and fungus-like microbes. Adapting its connection to the plant’s defense machinery improved protection, with no detected fruit-yield penalty in the experiment.
sources.quote: Overall, these results demonstrate that stable ectopic expression of RLP23 in tomato promotes broad-spectrum resistance to destructive bacterial, fungal and oomycete pathogens.
sources.cited_for: Receptor transfer and engineering can improve protection against different kinds of disease-causing microbes in tomatoes.
sources.not_established: The experiments did not establish predictable protection across crop families or lasting protection in fields.

sources.who: Stella Cesari, Yuxuan Xi, Nathalie Declerck and colleagues
sources.showed: An engineered receptor recognized an additional fungal protein in a laboratory plant. The change did not extend disease resistance in rice plants.
sources.quote: By introducing into RGA5_HMA the AVR-PikD binding residues of Pikp-1_HMA, we create a high-affinity binding surface for this effector.
sources.cited_for: Engineering recognition alone does not guarantee protection in the intended crop.
sources.not_established: The altered receptor did not turn its expanded recognition into expanded disease resistance in rice.

shown: Yang and colleagues demonstrated improved tomato resistance in controlled infection studies. Their work also strengthened immune signaling in isolated rice cells and fungal resistance in poplar leaves that temporarily produced the receptor. Those results do not establish protection in whole rice plants or lasting resistance in trees.
missing: A predictable design process has yet to produce whole-plant resistance across unrelated disease groups and crop families.
Engineered protection still needs to withstand changing disease-causing microbes across seasons and field locations.
Protection must preserve growth and harvestable yield across varieties and conditions, with acceptable effects on beneficial organisms.

milestones.label: Predictable resistance across disease groups and crop families
milestones.explanation: Independent groups would have to use a documented process to predict and produce whole-plant resistance across unrelated disease groups and crop families. This would establish that the design process transfers reliably.

milestones.label: Resistance lasts across seasons and locations
milestones.explanation: Field trials would have to compare engineered crops with susceptible and resistant crops across seasons and locations while tracking microbial changes and escape. This would test whether protection lasts under farm conditions.

milestones.label: Reproducible crop benefits meet predefined thresholds
milestones.explanation: Reproducible trials would have to measure disease, yield, development, defense costs and effects on beneficial organisms against predefined thresholds. This would establish practical value with acceptable tradeoffs.

milestones.label: Demonstrated breadth and durability have clearly stated limits
milestones.explanation: Results would have to specify tested crops, varieties, microbes, environments and duration, including failures and needed adaptations. This would define the protection demonstrated without implying permanent or universal immunity.

uncertain: How readily can disease-causing microbes evade the chosen warning signs or overcome the resulting defenses?
Which success thresholds, trial durations and yield or ecological tradeoffs are appropriate for each crop and disease?
How well will engineered defenses preserve beneficial relationships with microbes?

page.title: Engineered broad-spectrum, durable crop disease resistance
page.definition: Crop immune receptors, proteins that detect microbial molecules and activate defence, can be designed or adapted to resist specified pathogens from different microbial groups in different crops. Resistance preserves productivity and remains effective during prolonged, widespread cultivation under conditions favourable to those diseases.

goal.need: An expert survey covering 137 crop pathogens and pests collected 989 reports from 219 specialists in 67 countries between 1 November 2016 and 31 January 2017. Estimated global yield losses ranged from 17.2% for potato to 30.0% for rice. These estimates include animal pests; they cannot be attributed wholly to diseases or treated as losses recoverable by receptor engineering.

figures.caption: Estimated global yield losses from pathogens and pests
figures.note: Estimates from the expert survey, rather than measurements from a single field experiment.

completion.title: Designed crop immunity retains disease protection and productivity through prolonged, widespread cultivation.
completion.criterion: A receptor-design method produces resistance to specified pathogens from different microbial groups in different crop species. The engineered resistance reduces pathogen development or disease damage relative to susceptible varieties under comparable conditions, preserves crop productivity and fitness, and remains effective during prolonged, widespread cultivation in disease-conducive environments. Assessment is retrospective and limited to the crops, pathogen populations and cultivation histories demonstrated. The cited bodies specify no universal duration, area or permissible yield penalty.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of USDA-ARS and developer goals, ISF resistance terminology and the plant-pathology convention for durability.
completion.basis: Searched USDA-ARS NP303, National Academies crop recommendations, ISF definitions, CGIAR readiness frameworks and receptor-engineering papers; found no operational test combining programmable recognition, cross-crop breadth, productivity and durability. This synthesis combines the stated goals with Johnson's field definition of durability, as discussed by Lo Iacono and colleagues. It is not an externally adopted certification.

milestones.title: Engineered receptors trigger a target-dependent immune response in plant tissue.
milestones.criterion: A receptor produces a target-dependent immune response above matched controls in plant tissue. Intracellular: Cesari et al., 21 March 2022, obtained AVR-PikD-triggered cell death with RGA4/RGA5m1m2 in Nicotiana benthamiana at 5 days, with 3 biological replicates and ANOVA/Tukey testing at 0.05. Cell-surface: Yang et al., 13 October 2025, measured increased ethylene 4 h after 2 µM nlp20 treatment in leaves expressing RLP23 chimeras (n=6; three experimental repetitions). These endpoints establish activation.
milestones.set_by: Cesari et al., published cell-death assay in Figure 7, developed for intracellular rice receptor pairs tested in Nicotiana benthamiana; Yang et al., Figure 2, supplies the cell-surface receptor activation assay.
milestones.threshold_quote: The RGA5m1m2 mutant recognizes AVR-Pia and AVR-PikD in N. benthamiana.

milestones.title: Engineered receptors reduce crop disease relative to susceptible controls.
milestones.criterion: Crop plants restrict pathogen growth or disease damage relative to susceptible controls under comparable conditions. Cell-surface: Yang et al. (13 October 2025) reduced Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato DC3000 growth (n=20) and Botrytis cinerea and Phytophthora infestans lesions (n=18 each) in tomato; fruit-yield assays (n=8 plants) detected no penalty. Intracellular: Cesari et al.'s 6 independent T1 RGA5-variant rice lines lacked AVR-PikD resistance. Zhu et al. (3 September 2026) report resistance in SPIR-expressing transgenic plants; their abstract gives no assay sample sizes.
milestones.set_by: International Seed Federation, September 2022 resistance definitions for vegetable and ornamental varieties. The comparative resistance test is applied here to engineered crops; the cited experiments were not certified under ISF resistance classes.
milestones.threshold_quote: IR plant varieties will still show less severe symptoms or damage than susceptible plant varieties

milestones.title: Engineered resistance survives three field seasons, including two seasons at multiple sites.
milestones.criterion: A receptor-engineered crop retains resistance through 3 field seasons, including 2 multilocation seasons, with agronomic comparison against its parent variety. Intracellular: Vic.172 potato resisted late blight in unsprayed trials; agronomic comparisons used 3 replicate plots per genotype per site, spanning March 2019 to January 2021. Cell-surface: EFR tomato has field efficacy evidence at 2 Florida sites; the opened abstract does not establish this 3-season benchmark. The potato results concern transferred natural receptors and one pathogen species, not programmed resistance across pathogen groups.
milestones.set_by: International Potato Center, published successful-piloting assessment in CGIAR MEL innovation 478. This field-season benchmark was used for potato late-blight resistance, not established as a universal crop requirement.
milestones.threshold_quote: three seasons in the field, two seasons of multilocational confined field trials

milestones.title: Farmers outside the development network cultivate receptor-engineered crops.
milestones.criterion: Farmers unconnected with the development programme cultivate receptor-engineered crop varieties. This corresponds to Scaling Readiness innovation-use level 8, which requires use by stakeholders outside the innovation's development network. Research-managed demonstration plots or seed availability alone do not establish this endpoint. The framework specifies no minimum farmer count or cultivated area. This adoption test applies separately to cell-surface and intracellular receptor approaches.
milestones.set_by: Sartas and colleagues, Scaling Readiness agricultural-innovation assessment framework, Table 2, innovation-use level 8. The criterion is stated in that table; its application to receptor-engineered varieties is an Atlas mapping.

not_found: No public farmer-adoption evidence was located for receptor designs meeting the combined completion criterion in either receptor class.
The full texts of Zhu et al.'s 2026 SPIR study and Kunwar et al.'s 2018 field study could not be opened; their opened abstracts provide no plant-level sample sizes.

results.finding: Six independent T1 rice lines with engineered RGA5 variants did not gain AVR-PikD resistance.
results.detail: The variants retained resistance to naturally recognized effectors. In T2 tests, AVR-PikD lesions were not smaller than those in control rice lines; the intended new resistance was not achieved.
results.quote: These experiments show that in the transgenic RGA5m1, m2, and m1m2 plants disease lesions caused by Guy11_AVR-PikD are not reduced in size compared to the control rice lines or to infection with the Guy11_EV isolate.

results.finding: Synthetic plant immune receptors showed target specificity and immune activation; sample size and response magnitude not reported.
results.detail: Binding modules were grafted into an integrated decoy domain, but the abstract does not report a matched-control comparison or quantitative activation results.
results.quote: Their performance was improved by combining artificial intelligence-guided protein design with in planta-directed evolution, enhancing immune activation while reducing autoactivation.
